# hoba — Hiring Obstacles & Barriers Atlas

> A public, versioned, machine-readable registry of what goes wrong in hiring and what can be inferred from it. Registry 2026.08.2, schema 1.1.0. Content CC BY-SA 4.0, code MIT.

hoba separates an observation from its cause. A rejection email is a signal; the mechanisms that could have produced it are a separate layer; which of them a candidate can act on is a third. The registry never asserts which mechanism fired — only which are compatible, and which probes distinguish them.

## Ontology

- **Observations** (`A-*`, 14) — signals a candidate can actually witness.
- **Barriers** (`B-*`, 14) — the funnel gates, a strict DAG ordered by stage.
- **Mechanisms** (`M-*`, 24) — causes that can emit those signals, each with an actor, a nature, a visibility and a removability.
- **Patterns** (`P-*`, 4) — named motifs where several defensible decisions combine into a bind.
- **Loops** (`L-*`, 3) — reinforcing cycles, detected as strongly connected components.
- **Interventions** (`I-*`, 6) — concrete changes, each attributed to the actor who can make it.
- **Eras** (`E-*`, 4) — periods of the hiring economy, told as where the money came from and how a person got in.
- **Evidence** (`EVD-*`, 29) — the published sources behind the claims.

The graph has 65 nodes and 199 edges over the relations `operates_at`, `emits`, `amplifies`, `masks`, `precedes`, `instantiates`, `targets`, `mitigates`.

## Reading it by machine

- Full registry: https://hoba.work/data/latest/registry.json
- One entity: https://hoba.work/api/v1/mechanisms/M-001.json
- Any page as Markdown: https://hoba.work/mechanisms/M-001.md — or the canonical URL with `Accept: text/markdown`
- The whole catalogue as one document: https://hoba.work/registry.md
- Graph: https://hoba.work/data/latest/graph.json · https://hoba.work/data/latest/graph.graphml
- Tabular: https://hoba.work/data/latest/nodes.csv · https://hoba.work/data/latest/edges.csv
- Schema: https://hoba.work/data/latest/schema.json · OpenAPI: https://hoba.work/openapi.json
- This file in full: https://hoba.work/llms-full.txt

An MCP server ships in the repository (`packages/mcp`) exposing search, entity lookup, the diagnostic protocol, pattern matching and graph traversal over stdio.

## What it will not do

- It does not name or rank employers, and it holds no company records.
- It does not attribute intent. Mechanisms describe structure, not motive.
- Document excerpts on the site are reconstructions, written to be typical, and are labelled as such. They are not captured records.

---

## Observations

### A-001 — Complete silence after submission

No automated receipt, acknowledgement, rejection, or recruiter outreach is received following application submission.

- Stages: ingestion, sourcing · Evidence: supported
- Does NOT establish: Does not prove the application was reviewed by a human.
- Does NOT establish: Does not prove the role was cancelled or already filled.
- Probe [PROBE-A-001-1] (low): Check email spam and security quarantine folders for ATS automated acknowledgement tokens. → Confirms whether application was ingested and generated a confirmation ID.

### A-002 — Generic "closer alignment" rejection template

Standard automated email stating the team decided to proceed with candidates whose profiles more closely match role requirements.

- Stages: screening, recruiter, technical · Evidence: supported
- Does NOT establish: Does not establish which specific skill was deemed insufficient.
- Does NOT establish: Does not establish whether a human reviewer read the full resume.
- Probe [PROBE-A-002-1] (low): Compare CV keyword density with exact requirement phrases in the published job description. → Reveals potential vocabulary mismatch between candidate phrasing and ATS rubric.

### A-003 — Position closed after final interview without hire

Candidate completes all interview rounds, but is informed that the requisition has been cancelled, frozen, or closed.

- Stages: team, offer · Evidence: supported
- Does NOT establish: Does not prove candidate failed technical or behavioral evaluations.
- Does NOT establish: Does not prove the company lied about opening intention.
- Probe [PROBE-A-003-1] (low): Politely inquire with recruiter if the position was closed due to business budget restructuring or team reallocation. → Clarifies whether barrier was candidate-specific or macroeconomic/budgetary.

### A-004 — Materially similar role reposted shortly after rejection

Candidate observes the same or near-identical job listing reposted or refreshed on job boards within 1–8 weeks of rejection.

- Stages: sourcing, screening, technical · Evidence: supported
- Does NOT establish: Does not establish that the role was a "fake" or "ghost" posting.
- Does NOT establish: Does not establish that the prior interview feedback was fraudulent.
- Probe [PROBE-A-004-1] (low): Check job listing requisition ID or ask recruiter whether the posting is an automated ATS refresh or a distinct headcount opening. → Distinguishes between automated job board bot refreshes and genuine recurring hiring demand.

### A-005 — Compensation band reduced or altered mid-process

Offered or discussed compensation band is revised downward from previously agreed or advertised range.

- Stages: recruiter, compensation, offer · Evidence: supported
- Does NOT establish: Does not prove intentional bait-and-switch malice unless verified by company policy evidence.
- Probe [PROBE-A-005-1] (medium): Request clarification on whether the revised band reflects a lower leveling grade or a company-wide budget adjustment. → Separates leveling evaluation outcome from company financial constraints.

### A-006 — Take-home assignment exceeding reasonable stated scope

Take-home assignment requires building complex production-grade features demanding 20+ hours instead of stated 2–4 hours.

- Stages: technical · Evidence: supported
- Does NOT establish: Does not prove the company is harvesting free intellectual property for production use.
- Probe [PROBE-A-006-1] (low): Define explicit boundaries and trade-offs in submission README stating assumptions made to fit the agreed timebox. → Tests whether evaluators value scope management and communication over unbounded free work.

### A-007 — Multiple interview reschedulings or interviewer no-show

Interviews are repeatedly postponed, delayed at short notice, or interviewer fails to join scheduled call.

- Stages: recruiter, technical, team · Evidence: supported
- Does NOT establish: Does not imply candidate rejection; frequently reflects interviewer calendar congestion or emergency incidents.
- Probe [PROBE-A-007-1] (low): Offer clear flexible availability slots and confirm contact details 2 hours prior to the call. → Minimizes scheduling friction and verifies recruiter responsiveness.

### A-008 — Explicit feedback citing skill-depth shortfall

Interviewer or recruiter provides structured notes citing a specific deficit in algorithmic complexity, architecture, or tool mastery.

- Stages: technical, team · Evidence: supported
- Does NOT establish: Does not imply general incompetence; reflects threshold for this specific role level.
- Probe [PROBE-A-008-1] (medium): Review interview problem solution against industry standard patterns and identify edge cases missed. → Verifies whether candidate code truly lacked required optimization or rigor.

### A-009 — Rejection within minutes of application submission

Automated rejection email arrives within 2 to 30 minutes of form submission, outside human business hours.

- Stages: ingestion · Evidence: supported
- Does NOT establish: Does not imply candidate resume was judged as poor by human engineers.
- Probe [PROBE-A-009-1] (low): Audit application answers to mandatory knock-out questions (work permit, country of residence, minimum years experience). → Identifies exact boolean filter rule triggered by ATS.

### A-010 — Communication mismatch or tone friction in panel

Noticeable divergence in communication style, pacing, or terminology during live panel discussions.

- Stages: recruiter, team · Evidence: supported
- Does NOT establish: Does not prove candidate lacks teamwork skills globally.
- Probe [PROBE-A-010-1] (low): Request explicit feedback on collaborative dynamic from recruiter. → Clarifies whether friction was perceived as attitude issue or stylistic preference.

### A-011 — Offer rescinded or delayed due to internal freeze

Candidate is verbally offered a role or receives written offer which is subsequently delayed or retracted before start date.

- Stages: offer, post-offer · Evidence: supported
- Does NOT establish: Does not imply candidate failed reference checks unless explicitly stated.
- Probe [PROBE-A-011-1] (low): Request formal written notice regarding whether requisition is permanently cancelled or deferred to next fiscal quarter. → Provides timeline clarity for candidate decision-making.

### A-012 — Unsolicited recruiter outreach followed by ghosting

Recruiter initiates direct outreach expressing strong interest, but ceases communication after candidate responds with availability.

- Stages: sourcing, recruiter · Evidence: supported
- Does NOT establish: Does not prove candidate profile was rejected; often indicates batch automated sourcing campaigns.
- Probe [PROBE-A-012-1] (low): Send one single polite follow-up after 5 business days referencing original outreach thread. → Recovers stalled conversation if recruiter was out-of-office or overwhelmed.

### A-013 — Feedback stating candidate is overqualified for the grade

Candidate is rejected on the grounds that their experience, seniority, or previous scope exceeds the open position tier.

- Stages: recruiter, screening, team · Evidence: supported
- Does NOT establish: Does not imply the candidate is undesirable, but signals retention/flight-risk and compensation mismatch concerns.
- Probe [PROBE-A-013-1] (low): Inquire whether the organization has higher-tier or staff-level requisitions open where broader scope is desired. → Channels candidate into appropriate leveling track.

### A-014 — Conflicting feedback across different interviewers

Feedback from one round praises architectural depth while another round claims insufficient technical background.

- Stages: technical, team · Evidence: supported
- Does NOT establish: Does not prove bad faith; highlights lack of rubric calibration across the hiring committee.
- Probe [PROBE-A-014-1] (low): Request aggregated hiring rubric summary from talent partner. → Reveals whether team had misaligned internal evaluation criteria.

## Barriers

### B-013 — Requisition Approval & Public Posting

The gate that exists before any candidate does: headcount is authorized, the job description is written, and the requisition is published (or quietly kept open) on careers pages and job boards.

- Stage: pre-posting · Order: 1 · Passes when: An approved requisition with a written job description is published against real, funded headcount.
- Precedes: B-014, B-001

### B-014 — Outbound Sourcing & Talent Pool Contact

Recruiter-initiated outreach to passive candidates and talent-pool building, independent of any inbound application.

- Stage: sourcing · Order: 2 · Passes when: The candidate responds to outreach and is attached to an active, authorized requisition rather than a speculative pool.
- Precedes: B-001, B-004

### B-001 — Application Ingestion

The initial ingestion gate where candidate CV and structured application fields enter the talent acquisition database / ATS.

- Stage: ingestion · Order: 3 · Passes when: Application record is successfully received, validated for minimum schema, and linked to the active job requisition.
- Precedes: B-002

### B-002 — Automated Filter & Parser Threshold

Algorithmic text extraction, keyword scoring, compliance screening (location/work authorization), and knockout question evaluations.

- Stage: ingestion · Order: 4 · Passes when: CV parsing achieves sufficient extraction score and candidate passes all mandatory algorithmic gating rules.
- Precedes: B-003, B-004

### B-003 — Inbound Screening & Triage

Recruiter or sourcing coordinator manual review of parsed inbound applications vs active outbound talent pipelines.

- Stage: screening · Order: 5 · Passes when: Recruiter assigns application to the active short-list for initial conversational outreach.
- Precedes: B-004

### B-004 — Recruiter Screening Call

Initial conversational interview evaluating salary expectations, timeline, communication, English fluency, and high-level role alignment.

- Stage: recruiter · Order: 6 · Passes when: Recruiter and candidate align on core parameters and candidate is submitted to hiring team.
- Precedes: B-005

### B-005 — Technical Screen / Live Assessment

Synchronous technical evaluation assessing core technical competencies, problem-solving speed, and system architecture fundamentals.

- Stage: technical · Order: 7 · Passes when: Candidate achieves passing score on technical evaluation rubric from the assessing engineer.
- Precedes: B-006, B-007

### B-006 — Take-Home / Work Sample Evaluation

Asynchronous technical assignment or project artifact reviewed by engineering peers against quality benchmarks.

- Stage: technical · Order: 8 · Passes when: Code artifact satisfies architectural, functional, test coverage, and documentation requirements.
- Precedes: B-007

### B-007 — Hiring Manager In-Depth Review

Detailed evaluation of candidate seniority, project ownership history, trade-off reasoning, and team-specific mission fit.

- Stage: hiring-manager · Order: 9 · Passes when: Hiring manager confirms candidate has required depth and approves progression to final panel.
- Precedes: B-008

### B-008 — Team & Cross-Functional Panel

Multi-interviewer round assessing collaborative problem solving, code review etiquette, cross-functional communication, and cultural norms.

- Stage: team · Order: 10 · Passes when: Consensus score among team panelists meets or exceeds hire recommendation threshold.
- Precedes: B-009

### B-009 — Compensation & Leveling Reconciliation

Internal alignment between candidate expected compensation/level and company pay bands / leveling grid.

- Stage: compensation · Order: 11 · Passes when: Candidate expectations fit within approved salary band and equity guidelines for the target grade.
- Precedes: B-010

### B-010 — Headcount & Executive Budget Approval

Formal sign-off by department leadership, finance, and talent committee to commit budget for the written offer.

- Stage: offer · Order: 12 · Passes when: Active headcount requisition is formally certified and unblocked by financial leadership.
- Precedes: B-011

### B-011 — Reference & Background Verification

Third-party or internal verification of past employment records, academic degrees, and professional references.

- Stage: post-offer · Order: 13 · Passes when: All mandatory background checks clear with no unresolved factual discrepancies.
- Precedes: B-012

### B-012 — Offer Closing & Contract Execution

Final mutual execution of the formal employment agreement and start-date confirmation.

- Stage: post-offer · Order: 14 · Passes when: Both parties sign offer contract and onboarding workflow is triggered.

## Mechanisms

### M-001 — Genuine Technical Skill Shortfall

The candidate’s verified technical execution or domain depth does not meet the established baseline for the role level.

- Actor: candidate · Nature: rule · Visibility: inferable · Removability: candidate
- Operates at: B-005, B-006, B-007 · honest baseline
- Emits: A-008 (direct), A-002 (euphemism)
- Does NOT establish: Rejection does not mean the candidate has no engineering ability, only that the requirement bar was unmet for this specific benchmark.

### M-002 — Stronger Competing Candidate in Final Cohort

Candidate cleared all passing bars, but another applicant in the same pipeline demonstrated superior domain overlap or lower onboarding overhead.

- Actor: candidate · Nature: rule · Visibility: opaque · Removability: none
- Operates at: B-007, B-008, B-010 · honest baseline
- Emits: A-002 (euphemism), A-003 (distortion)
- Does NOT establish: Does not mean candidate had negative feedback; relative cohort ranking is outside candidate control.

### M-003 — ATS Parser Extraction Failure

Multi-column formatting, graphics, custom fonts, or unsupported document layouts cause ATS parser to corrupt or omit critical work history.

- Actor: system · Nature: noise · Visibility: inferable · Removability: candidate
- Operates at: B-001, B-002
- Emits: A-001 (void), A-009 (direct)
- Does NOT establish: Does not imply human recruiter evaluated and disliked candidate experience.

### M-004 — Unstated Compensation Band Discrepancy

Candidate market rate exceeds budgeted compensation for the requisition, but salary band was never published or clarified early.

- Actor: policy · Nature: rule · Visibility: opaque · Removability: intermediary
- Operates at: B-004, B-009
- Emits: A-002 (euphemism), A-005 (direct), A-013 (euphemism)
- Does NOT establish: Rejection does not mean candidate is overpriced for the market, only mismatched with this specific employer budget.

### M-005 — Pre-Selected Internal Candidate

Requisition was publicly advertised to satisfy corporate policy or legal compliance while an internal employee was already earmarked for the role.

- Actor: policy · Nature: incentive · Visibility: opaque · Removability: none
- Operates at: B-013, B-001, B-003, B-007
- Emits: A-002 (euphemism), A-003 (euphemism)
- Does NOT establish: Cannot be asserted as fact without internal hiring log confirmation.

### M-006 — Stale or Orphaned Job Requisition

Job posting remains active on careers page and aggregator portals despite the team having ceased active hiring or closed headcount.

- Actor: system · Nature: void · Visibility: opaque · Removability: none
- Operates at: B-013, B-001, B-002, B-003
- Emits: A-001 (void), A-004 (noise)
- Does NOT establish: Application silence does not reflect candidate suitability.

### M-007 — Headcount Freeze or Budget Cancellation

Executive leadership or finance halts all new hires across division due to macroeconomic factors or revenue shifts mid-interview process.

- Actor: policy · Nature: rule · Visibility: inferable · Removability: none
- Operates at: B-008, B-010, B-012
- Emits: A-003 (direct), A-011 (direct)
- Does NOT establish: Candidate performance in interview was not the causal trigger for process termination.

### M-008 — Automated Keyword / Qualification Filter

Deterministic filter rejecting applications missing exact acronyms, certifications, or specific years-of-experience thresholds.

- Actor: system · Nature: rule · Visibility: inferable · Removability: candidate
- Operates at: B-002
- Emits: A-009 (direct), A-002 (euphemism)
- Does NOT establish: Passing keyword filters does not guarantee interview invitation.

### M-009 — Recruiter Volume & Quota Incentive Distortion

Recruiters optimize for pipeline velocity and superficial pattern-matching due to overwhelming applicant volume (500+ per req).

- Actor: recruiter · Nature: incentive · Visibility: inferable · Removability: intermediary
- Operates at: B-003, B-004
- Emits: A-001 (void), A-012 (noise)
- Does NOT establish: Does not mean recruiter is individually negligent; reflects structural capacity mismatch.

### M-010 — Hidden Evaluation Rubric or Undisclosed Priority

The interview team grades candidate against specific undisclosed architectural dogmas, internal frameworks, or unwritten biases.

- Actor: hiring-manager · Nature: bias · Visibility: opaque · Removability: intermediary
- Operates at: B-005, B-007, B-008
- Emits: A-008 (distortion), A-014 (direct)
- Does NOT establish: Failure to guess unstated preferences is not equivalent to lack of core competence.

### M-011 — Employment Gap Downranking Bias

Automated ranking algorithms or human screeners discount candidates with recent career breaks regardless of verified project history.

- Actor: system · Nature: bias · Visibility: inferable · Removability: none
- Operates at: B-002, B-003
- Emits: A-001 (void), A-002 (euphemism)
- Does NOT establish: Employment gap does not correlate with underlying technical decline.

### M-012 — Interview Resource & Scheduling Saturation

Engineering interviewers are overwhelmed with sprint commitments, leading to calendar fragmentation, rush reviews, or dropped loops.

- Actor: hiring-manager · Nature: noise · Visibility: inferable · Removability: intermediary
- Operates at: B-005, B-007, B-008
- Emits: A-007 (direct), A-001 (noise)
- Does NOT establish: Rescheduling is an operational issue and does not indicate negative evaluation.

### M-013 — Mid-Process Role Requirement Redefinition

Team changes tech stack, seniority requirements, or project scope mid-funnel, invalidating previous interview assessments.

- Actor: hiring-manager · Nature: noise · Visibility: inferable · Removability: none
- Operates at: B-007, B-008, B-009
- Emits: A-003 (distortion), A-004 (direct)
- Does NOT establish: Candidate rejection was driven by shifting team mandate, not prior interview answers.

### M-014 — Location or Timezone Compliance Constraint

Company legal or tax entity cannot support remote employment contracts in candidate physical residency jurisdiction.

- Actor: policy · Nature: rule · Visibility: observable · Removability: intermediary
- Operates at: B-002, B-004
- Emits: A-009 (direct), A-002 (euphemism)
- Does NOT establish: Legal geography barrier is completely independent of candidate technical competence.

### M-015 — Communication or Working Style Friction

Candidate demonstrated abrasive tone, defensive reactions to critique, or inability to listen during collaborative interview problem solving.

- Actor: candidate · Nature: bias · Visibility: observable · Removability: candidate
- Operates at: B-004, B-008 · honest baseline
- Emits: A-010 (direct), A-002 (euphemism)
- Does NOT establish: Style friction during high-stress interview is not a permanent personality defect.

### M-016 — Speculative Sourcing / Talent Pooling Without Opening

Recruiters proactively gather candidate pools for future anticipated headcount that is not yet authorized or funded.

- Actor: recruiter · Nature: incentive · Visibility: opaque · Removability: none
- Operates at: B-013, B-014, B-003, B-004
- Emits: A-012 (distortion), A-001 (void)
- Does NOT establish: Ghosting after outbound message indicates absence of immediate opening, not profile rejection.

### M-017 — Experience-Age Grading Mismatch

Candidate with 10+ years applied for mid/senior role, triggering fears of boredom, rapid churn, or salary dissatisfaction.

- Actor: recruiter · Nature: bias · Visibility: inferable · Removability: none
- Operates at: B-003, B-004, B-007
- Emits: A-013 (direct), A-002 (euphemism)
- Does NOT establish: Being rejected as "overqualified" is an organizational tier mismatch, not a candidate deficiency.

### M-018 — Domain Specificity Over-Weighting

Interviewer requires exact vertical experience (e.g. adtech, crypto, specific payment processor) over deep transferable systems fundamentals.

- Actor: hiring-manager · Nature: bias · Visibility: inferable · Removability: intermediary
- Operates at: B-004, B-007
- Emits: A-002 (euphemism), A-008 (direct)
- Does NOT establish: Transferable general engineering skills are not disproven by lack of specific proprietary protocol knowledge.

### M-019 — Take-Home Evaluation Fatigue & Asymmetry

Reviewers perform hurried 5-minute scans of complex 15-hour take-home projects, missing subtle architectural patterns and tests.

- Actor: hiring-manager · Nature: noise · Visibility: opaque · Removability: none
- Operates at: B-006
- Emits: A-006 (noise), A-002 (euphemism)
- Does NOT establish: Take-home rejection under evaluation fatigue does not measure true software engineering craftsmanship.

### M-020 — Automated Application Expiration Timeout

ATS configuration automatically issues bulk rejections to all pending unreviewed applications after 45 or 60 days.

- Actor: system · Nature: rule · Visibility: opaque · Removability: none
- Operates at: B-001, B-003
- Emits: A-002 (void), A-001 (void)
- Does NOT establish: Bulk timeout rejection contains zero qualitative assessment of candidate profile.

### M-021 — Reference Check Discrepancy or Regulatory Ineligibility

Third-party check reveals unverified employment dates, unconfirmed degrees, or direct conflict of interest.

- Actor: candidate · Nature: rule · Visibility: observable · Removability: candidate
- Operates at: B-011 · honest baseline
- Emits: A-011 (direct), A-002 (euphemism)
- Does NOT establish: Administrative mismatch in dates is distinct from fraudulent resume misrepresentation.

### M-022 — Hiring Manager Consensus Impasse

The interview panel splits 50/50 without an executive tiebreaker, defaulting conservatively to a "no-hire" decision.

- Actor: hiring-manager · Nature: bias · Visibility: opaque · Removability: none
- Operates at: B-008
- Emits: A-014 (direct), A-002 (euphemism)
- Does NOT establish: Split panel reflects lack of calibrated internal standards rather than candidate failure.

### M-023 — Portfolio / Work Artifact Misinterpretation

Screeners overlook candidate role architecture due to non-standard repository layout or unindexed open-source contributions.

- Actor: candidate · Nature: noise · Visibility: inferable · Removability: candidate
- Operates at: B-003, B-005
- Emits: A-002 (euphemism), A-008 (distortion)
- Does NOT establish: Misinterpreted architecture can be corrected through structured documentation.

### M-024 — Inflated Requisition Requirements vs Actual Team Needs

Job description demands 10+ niche technologies and Staff-level qualifications for a straightforward feature engineering role.

- Actor: hiring-manager · Nature: incentive · Visibility: inferable · Removability: intermediary
- Operates at: B-013, B-002, B-004
- Emits: A-002 (euphemism), A-004 (noise)
- Does NOT establish: Failing to meet an inflated "wishlist" does not mean candidate cannot excel at the team’s actual core tasks.

## Patterns

### P-001 — Seniority Double Bind

Candidate is simultaneously rejected as overqualified for junior/mid roles and underqualified (or insufficiently specialized) for staff/leadership roles.

- Triggers when: Candidate observes rejection for overqualification at level N and skill-depth shortfall at level N+1 within the same market cycle.
- Requires: A-002, A-013 · Mechanisms: M-001, M-004, M-017
- Establishes: Candidate falls into an evaluation boundary gap where compensation/experience expectations mismatch standard job tiers.
- Does NOT establish: Does not establish that the candidate lacks market value.
- Does NOT establish: Does not establish malice or coordinated collusion between employers.

### P-002 — Closed-Then-Reposted Requisition Motif

A candidate completes multiple late-stage interviews, is rejected with a generic message, and sees the identical role reposted weeks later.

- Triggers when: Candidate observes role closure/rejection followed by public reopening of materially similar role listing within 60 days.
- Requires: A-003, A-004 · Mechanisms: M-002, M-006, M-010, M-013
- Establishes: The requisition requirements or target profile were not satisfied by the interviewed pool, or search criteria changed mid-process.
- Does NOT establish: Does not establish that the original job listing was fake or a ghost job.
- Does NOT establish: Does not establish that candidate was intentionally misled.

### P-003 — Experience-Age Impossibility

Requisition requires more years of hands-on experience in a specific framework or tool than that technology has existed in the open-source ecosystem.

- Triggers when: Job description or automated screen requires X years of experience where X > technology_age.
- Requires: A-002, A-009 · Mechanisms: M-008, M-024
- Establishes: Job description was authored without technical review, using copy-paste templates with automated gating rules.
- Does NOT establish: Does not imply technical team is incompetent, only that HR screening pipeline lacks technical validation.

### P-004 — Compensation Double Bind

Candidate is required to state salary expectation first; quoting high triggers immediate rejection, while quoting low triggers leveling downranking.

- Triggers when: Asymmetric salary inquiry where employer refuses band disclosure prior to candidate submitting binding number.
- Requires: A-002, A-005 · Mechanisms: M-004, M-017
- Establishes: Information asymmetry is utilized as an uncalibrated gatekeeper before technical merit is evaluated.
- Does NOT establish: Does not mean employer has unlimited budget or malice.

## Loops

### L-001 — Employment Gap Penalty Loop

An employment gap triggers automated downranking (M-011), which pushes the profile below keyword and qualification filters (M-008); fewer interview invitations lengthen the gap, which in turn strengthens the downranking.

- M-011 amplifies M-008
- M-008 amplifies M-011

### L-002 — Take-Home Opportunity-Cost Saturation Loop

Candidates invest heavy hours into unbounded take-home assignments, reducing bandwidth for applications, while reviewers suffer evaluation fatigue.

- M-012 amplifies M-019
- M-019 amplifies M-012

### L-003 — Inflated-Requirements Search Saturation Loop

Teams write inflated requirements, filtering out strong generalists, prolonging open search, causing recruiter fatigue and mid-process role redefinitions.

- M-024 amplifies M-008
- M-008 amplifies M-013
- M-013 amplifies M-024

## Interventions

### I-001 — Auto-Close Stale Job Requisitions

Implement automated ATS policy to expire public listings when headcount authorization lapses or no interview activity occurs within 60 days.

- Actor: employer-policy · Scope: organizational · Cost: low
- Targets: M-006, B-001, P-002, L-003
- Expected: Reduce stale public listings and candidate application waste
- Expected: Reduce ambiguous post-application silence

### I-002 — Upfront Compensation Band Disclosure

Publish verified salary and equity bands directly in job descriptions or disclose them prior to scheduling technical interview rounds.

- Actor: employer-policy · Scope: industry · Cost: low
- Targets: M-004, B-004, B-009, P-001, P-004
- Expected: Eliminate late-stage compensation mismatch dropouts
- Expected: Reduce time wasted on mismatched leveling conversations

### I-003 — Standardized Late-Stage Rejection Feedback Taxonomy

Provide candidates reaching technical or panel stages with structured, rubric-based feedback categories rather than generic templates.

- Actor: recruiter-process · Scope: organizational · Cost: medium
- Targets: M-001, M-010, B-007, B-008, P-001, P-002, L-003
- Expected: Provide actionable feedback signals to candidates
- Expected: Enforce consistent interviewer calibration across rounds

### I-004 — Remove Career Gap Feature from Automated Ranking Models

Disable employment duration gap penalties in recruitment AI algorithms and screening models.

- Actor: ats-vendor · Scope: ecosystem · Cost: low
- Targets: M-011, L-001
- Expected: Break algorithmic unemployment penalty loop
- Expected: Broaden candidate pool to include skilled returning talent

### I-005 — Candidate ATS Parser Conformance Test Utility

Provide candidates with an open-source parsing validation tool to verify CV machine-readability before submission.

- Actor: candidate-action · Scope: individual · Cost: low
- Targets: M-003, B-002, P-003
- Expected: Eliminate formatting-induced silent parsing failures
- Expected: Increase candidate confidence in resume ingestion fidelity

### I-006 — Strict Take-Home Timebox & Blinded Evaluation Rubric

Enforce strict 3-hour scope limits on take-homes, compensate candidates for extended samples, and grade submissions blind.

- Actor: hiring-manager · Scope: organizational · Cost: medium
- Targets: M-019, L-002, B-006
- Expected: Prevent reviewer fatigue and asymmetric code evaluation
- Expected: Respect candidate time investment and eliminate IP exploitation concerns

## Eras

### E-001 — Zero rates and a same-year deduction

For over a decade money cost nothing to borrow and engineering payroll reduced taxable income in the year it was paid. Both facts were policy, both were durable, and together they made an empty seat more expensive than a wrong hire.

- Span: 2008–2019
- The money: From 16 December 2008 the US policy rate sat at its floor for seven years, and the euro-area deposit rate was cut to zero in July 2012 and below zero in June 2014. Under section 174 as it then stood, research and experimental expenditures could be deducted in the year they were paid rather than charged to capital account. Borrowing to fund growth was close to free, and payroll spent building product reduced taxable income immediately.
- What it did to hiring: Headcount was the standard use of raised capital. A salary was a current-year deduction and the return on a hire was measured in growth rather than in margin, so teams were sized to a funded plan and the plan came before the revenue. A listing route stayed open to companies without trailing profits throughout the period, which meant payroll could run ahead of earnings without closing off the exit.
- How you got in: Demand for people who could do the work ran ahead of supply, so employers hired for potential and trained afterwards. A beginner's salary carried the same immediate deduction as a senior's, which made junior seats cheap to fund against the cost of leaving a seat empty. Self-teaching, a short conversion course and a first job with training attached were ordinary routes in.
- What closed it: Not by a contraction. In March 2020 the same policy floor was reimposed and fund flows stepped up by a multiple, and hiring plans were sized to capital raised rather than to current revenue.
- 0.00–0.25% — US federal funds target range, held at its floor (16 Dec 2008 – 15 Dec 2015, EVD-007)
- 0.00% → −0.50% — ECB deposit facility rate, at or below zero (11 Jul 2012 – 26 Jul 2022, EVD-008)
- 100% — Research and development payroll deductible in the year it was paid (to tax year 2021, EVD-012)
- 15–43% a year — US technology listings profitable on trailing earnings (2011–2021, EVD-011)

### E-002 — The record funding years

Two years in which the policy floor returned and venture funding roughly doubled its previous record. Headcount plans were set against committed capital rather than against bookings, and the terms of entry were set on the candidate's side.

- Span: 2020–2021
- The money: The policy rate returned to 0.00–0.25% on 16 March 2020 and stayed there for two years. US venture-backed companies raised $329.6 billion in 2021 against a previous record of $166.6 billion in 2020, and global venture investment reached $671 billion. The listing window stayed open to companies without earnings: of 121 US technology listings in 2021, 21% were profitable on trailing twelve-month earnings.
- What it did to hiring: With several years of funding raised at once, headcount was planned against committed capital rather than against bookings, and roles were opened before the work that would fill them was specified. Time-to-fill became the operative constraint, so loops were shortened, offers raised and candidate pools widened across locations. Recruiting functions were themselves staffed to the expanded plan.
- How you got in: Employers competed for candidates, so entry terms were set on the candidate's side: compressed interview loops, offers made on shorter evidence, and pay set by competing bids. Entry-level and career-change intake ran at volume, because the alternative was leaving funded seats empty. Holding a current job was not a precondition, and changing employer was the ordinary way to raise pay.
- What closed it: Two dated changes. The target range left the floor on 17 March 2022, and for tax years beginning after 31 December 2021 any amount paid in connection with developing software had to be capitalised and amortised over five years — so a developer's salary stopped reducing taxable income in the year it was paid.
- $329.6B — US venture-backed companies raised (2021, against $166.6B in 2020, EVD-009)
- $671B — Global venture capital invested (2021, EVD-010)
- 0.00–0.25% — US policy rate, back at its floor (16 Mar 2020 – 16 Mar 2022, EVD-007)
- 21% of 121 — US technology listings profitable on trailing earnings (2021, EVD-011)

### E-003 — Rates up, payroll repriced

The policy rate reached its cycle peak, technology equities repriced, every stage of the private funding chain contracted at once, and software payroll became something to amortise rather than deduct. The correction ran through announced reductions rather than through attrition.

- Span: 2022–2023
- The money: The federal funds target range reached a cycle peak of 5.25–5.50% effective 27 July 2023 and was held there for about fourteen months, and the technology-weighted NASDAQ Composite fell 36.4% from its November 2021 close to its December 2022 low. Every stage of the private chain contracted together: US venture deal value fell from $348.0 billion in 2021 to $170.6 billion in 2023, exit value hit a decade low of $61.5 billion, and new fund commitments fell to a six-year low of $66.9 billion. From tax years beginning after 31 December 2021, software development costs were amortised over five years for domestic research and fifteen for foreign research instead of being deducted when paid.
- What it did to hiring: Payroll was now both harder to refinance and slower to deduct, so plans were cut to the capital already in hand. Reductions were announced rather than absorbed through attrition: a tracker of publicly reported technology layoffs records 165,269 employees in 2022 and 265,660 in 2023, its highest year. Open requisitions were closed as well as filled positions eliminated, and the recruiting capacity built for the previous era was itself reduced.
- How you got in: Hiring narrowed to the replacement of specific departures, which meant a posted role described work someone had recently been doing. The evidence employers would accept narrowed with it: recent experience in the same title, at similar scale, in the same stack. The routes that worked when employers hired for potential produced no offers, because the seats being filled were defined by an incumbent's job description rather than by a plan.
- What closed it: The financial conditions reversed without the reduction reversing. The target range came off its peak on 18 September 2024 and the immediate domestic deduction was restored by statute in July 2025, but the headcount removed during the correction was not restored — so the reduced level carried forward as the baseline rather than as a trough.
- 5.25–5.50% — Peak US federal funds target range (27 Jul 2023 – 18 Sep 2024, EVD-016)
- −36.4% — NASDAQ Composite, record close to cycle low (19 Nov 2021 – 28 Dec 2022, EVD-017)
- $348.0B → $170.6B — US venture deal value (2021 → 2023, EVD-018)
- $61.5B — US venture exit value, a decade low (2023, EVD-018)
- 5 years domestic, 15 foreign — Software payroll amortised rather than deducted (tax years from 2022, EVD-013)
- 165,269 → 265,660 — Tracked technology layoffs, not a census (2022 → 2023, EVD-023)

### E-004 — A fixed number of seats

The conditions that made hiring expensive were reversed; the number of positions was not. The contraction now runs through the hiring channel rather than the separation channel, which is why it is competition for a fixed and shrinking number of seats rather than a shortage of qualified people.

- Span: 2024–2026
- The money: The tax treatment that penalised payroll was undone: section 174A, added on 4 July 2025, allows domestic research expenditure to be deducted when paid for tax years beginning after 31 December 2024, balances capitalised under the 2022–2024 rules may be recovered in one year or over two, and smaller taxpayers may elect back to 2022. Policy rates came off their cycle peak in September 2024. The inputs that made hiring expensive were reversed. The number of positions was not.
- What it did to hiring: The contraction runs through the hiring channel, not the separation channel. Official gross hires in the US information sector fell from 1,270,000 in 2022 to 903,000 in 2025 — down 28.9% — while official layoffs and discharges in the same series were roughly flat at 451,000, 399,000, 395,000 and 447,000. Openings averaged 224,000 a month in 2022 and 121,000 in 2025, and stood at 90,000 in June 2026. Sector payrolls fell from 3,115,000 in November 2022 to 2,780,000 in July 2026.
- How you got in: Incumbents vacate few seats: the information-sector quits rate was 1.1% in June 2026 against 1.9% in June 2022, and the total-private hires rate 3.7% against 4.7%. Applications per open role rose from 116 in 2022 to 244 in 2025 across one platform's benchmark. Software postings ran 69.3% senior and 4.5% entry-level in the first quarter of 2026, and payroll records show employment of developers aged 22–25 down close to 20% from its late-2022 peak while older ages in the same occupation did not fall. Entry now means succeeding a specific incumbent rather than being trained into a funded seat.
- 100% — Immediate deduction restored for domestic research (tax years from 2025, EVD-015)
- 1,270,000 → 903,000 — Gross hires, US information sector (2022 → 2025, EVD-022)
- 451,000 → 447,000 — Layoffs and discharges, US information sector — roughly flat (2022 → 2025, EVD-021)
- 224,000/mo → 90,000 — Job openings, US information sector (2022 average → Jun 2026, EVD-020)
- 3,115,000 → 2,780,000 — Information-sector payrolls (Nov 2022 → Jul 2026, EVD-019)
- 1.9% → 1.1% — Quits rate, US information sector (Jun 2022 → Jun 2026, EVD-026)
- 4.7% → 3.7% — Hires rate, total private (Jun 2022 → Jun 2026, EVD-025)
- 116 → 244 — Applications received per open role, one platform's benchmark (2022 → 2025, EVD-027)
- 69.3% senior, 4.5% entry — Software postings by level, one job board (Q1 2026, EVD-028)
- ≈ −20% — Employment of software developers aged 22–25 (late 2022 → Sep 2025, EVD-029)
- 149,023 — Announced technology job cuts, not a census (Jan–Jul 2026, EVD-024)

## Evidence

### EVD-001 — Hidden Workers: Untapped Talent (HBS / Accenture)

Survey of 8,000 workers and 2,250 executives in the US, UK and Germany on automated hiring. 88% of employers agree that qualified high-skill candidates are vetted out of the process by applicant tracking systems because they do not match the exact criteria of the job description; the report attributes a large "hidden worker" population to configurable ATS exclusion rules and knock-out filters.

- Fuller, J. B., Raman, M., Sage-Gavin, E., & Hines, K. (2021). Hidden Workers: Untapped Talent. Harvard Business School Project on Managing the Future of Work & Accenture.
- https://www.hbs.edu/managing-the-future-of-work/research/hidden-workers-untapped-talent

### EVD-002 — Too Good to Hire? Capability and Inferences about Commitment in Labor Markets

Four experiments with hiring managers show that candidates signalling more capability than the role requires are perceived as less committed to the organization and are penalized in hiring decisions — direct evidence for "overqualified" rejections and the seniority double bind.

- Galperin, R. V., Hahl, O., Sterling, A. D., & Guo, J. (2020). Administrative Science Quarterly, 65(2), 275–313.
- https://doi.org/10.1177/0001839219840022

### EVD-003 — Duration Dependence and Labor Market Conditions: Evidence from a Field Experiment

Field experiment sending roughly 12,000 fictitious résumés to about 3,000 postings in 100 US cities: the probability of an interview callback falls sharply with the length of the current unemployment spell (most of the decline within the first eight months) and the penalty is stronger in tighter labor markets — employers use gap length as a screening signal.

- Kroft, K., Lange, F., & Notowidigdo, M. J. (2013). The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 128(3), 1123–1167.
- https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjt015

### EVD-004 — Job Seekers Beware of Ghost Jobs (Clarify Capital survey of hiring managers)

Survey of 1,045 managers involved in hiring (fielded 31 Aug – 1 Sep 2022) on job postings kept live without active hiring: about half keep postings open because they are "always open to new people", 43% cite giving the impression that the company is growing or keeping existing employees motivated, one in three postings had been active for more than 30 days, and one in four respondents did not plan to fill the role for three months or longer.

- Clarify Capital (2022). Job Seekers Beware of Ghost Jobs. Survey of 1,045 hiring managers, 31 Aug – 1 Sep 2022.
- https://clarifycapital.com/job-seekers-beware-of-ghost-jobs-survey

### EVD-005 — Salary Transparency: Growth Slows, but Momentum Continues (Indeed Hiring Lab)

Tracks the share of US job postings on Indeed that disclose pay: 57.8% in September 2024, up from 52.2% a year earlier, with wide variation by occupation. Roughly four in ten postings still omit compensation — the structural precondition for compensation-band discrepancies surfacing only at late stages.

- Indeed Hiring Lab (2024, October 23). Salary Transparency: Growth Slows, but Momentum Continues.
- https://hiringlab.indeed.com/2024/10/23/salary-transparency-growth-slows-but-momentum-continues/

### EVD-006 — Employment Interview Reliability: New Meta-Analytic Estimates by Structure and Format

Meta-analysis of 125 inter-rater reliability coefficients (N = 32,428): reliability is substantially higher for panel interviews than for separate interviews by different interviewers (.74 vs .44) and rises with interview structure — quantifying how much interviewer variance, rather than candidate performance, drives divergent verdicts.

- Huffcutt, A. I., Culbertson, S. S., & Weyhrauch, W. S. (2013). International Journal of Selection and Assessment, 21(3), 264–276.
- https://doi.org/10.1111/ijsa.12036

### EVD-007 — Federal funds target range and effective rate (FRED)

The FOMC held the federal funds target range at 0.00–0.25% from 16 December 2008 to 15 December 2015 and again from 16 March 2020 to 16 March 2022. In every full month inside those two windows the effective federal funds rate stayed between 0.05% and 0.22%. Verified against the full daily DFEDTARU/DFEDTARL series (2,556 and 731 daily observations respectively, no other value in either window) and the monthly FEDFUNDS series.

- Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (US), Federal Funds Target Range — Upper Limit [DFEDTARU], Lower Limit [DFEDTARL] and Federal Funds Effective Rate [FEDFUNDS], retrieved from FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, 27 August 2026.
- https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTARU

### EVD-008 — ECB deposit facility rate (FRED)

The ECB deposit facility rate was cut to 0.00% on 11 July 2012, turned negative at −0.10% on 11 June 2014, reached −0.50% on 18 September 2019 and returned to 0.00% on 27 July 2022. Every one of the 3,668 daily observations between 11 July 2012 and 26 July 2022 is at or below zero.

- European Central Bank, ECB Deposit Facility Rate for Euro Area [ECBDFR], retrieved from FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, 27 August 2026.
- https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/ECBDFR

### EVD-009 — PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor, Q4 2021

US venture-backed companies raised $329.6 billion in 2021, against a previous record of $166.6 billion in 2020. The report states the figures verbatim; they are data-provider estimates and are revised in later vintages.

- PitchBook Data and National Venture Capital Association, Q4 2021 PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor, 13 January 2022.
- https://nvca.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/01/Q4_2021_PitchBook_NVCA_Venture_Monitor.pdf

### EVD-010 — KPMG Venture Pulse, Q4 2021

Global venture capital investment totalled $671 billion across 2021, the highest annual figure in the series, of which $171.4 billion was invested in Q4 2021 across 8,710 deals. Underlying data provided by PitchBook as of 31 December 2021.

- KPMG Private Enterprise, Venture Pulse Q4 2021: Global analysis of venture funding, 19 January 2022, p. 7.
- https://assets.kpmg.com/content/dam/kpmg/xx/pdf/2022/01/venture-pulse-q4-2021.pdf

### EVD-011 — Technology IPO profitability, 1980–2025 (Ritter)

Of 121 US technology listings in 2021, 21% were profitable on trailing- twelve-month earnings. The profitable share ranged from 15% to 43% in every year from 2011 to 2021, so a listing route remained open to companies without trailing profits throughout the period.

- Ritter, Jay R. (2026). Initial Public Offerings: Technology Stock IPOs, Table 4b — Technology and Life Science Company IPOs, 1980–2025. University of Florida.
- https://web.archive.org/web/20260731141233/https://site.warrington.ufl.edu/ritter/files/IPOs-Tech.pdf

### EVD-012 — 26 U.S.C. §174 as it stood before 2022

Under section 174(a)(1) as it stood before the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act took effect, a taxpayer could treat research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred in connection with a trade or business as expenses not chargeable to capital account, deductible in the year paid or incurred. Payroll spent on building product reduced taxable income in the same year it was spent.

- 26 U.S.C. §174, United States Code, 2017 Edition. U.S. Government Publishing Office.
- https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2017-title26/html/USCODE-2017-title26-subtitleA-chap1-subchapB-partVI-sec174.htm

### EVD-013 — 26 U.S.C. §174 after the 2017 amendment

Section 13206(a) of Public Law 115-97 rewrote section 174 to deny any current deduction for specified research or experimental expenditures and to require them to be charged to capital account and amortised ratably over five years beginning with the midpoint of the taxable year in which they are paid or incurred, effective for amounts paid or incurred in tax years beginning after 31 December 2021. Subsection (c)(3) treats any amount paid or incurred in connection with the development of software as such an expenditure, so roughly 10% of a developer's salary was deductible in the year it was paid.

- 26 U.S.C. §174, United States Code, 2023 Edition. U.S. Government Publishing Office. Amendment: Pub. L. 115-97 §13206(a).
- https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title26/html/USCODE-2023-title26-subtitleA-chap1-subchapB-partVI-sec174.htm

### EVD-014 — Rev. Proc. 2025-28 (IRS)

IRS guidance on the 2025 restoration: foreign research or experimental expenditures keep the 15-year amortisation period; balances capitalised under the 2022–2024 rules may be recovered in full in the first tax year beginning after 31 December 2024 or ratably over two years; and a taxpayer meeting the section 448(c) gross-receipts test — $31,000,000 average annual gross receipts over the three prior tax years for a year beginning in 2025 — may elect the new treatment retroactively to tax years beginning after 31 December 2021, by 6 July 2026.

- Internal Revenue Service, Rev. Proc. 2025-28, Internal Revenue Bulletin 2025-38, sections 2.02, 2.03(1), 2.06 and 3.02(1).
- https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rp-25-28.pdf

### EVD-015 — 26 U.S.C. §174A — domestic research expenditures

Section 70302(a) of Public Law 119-21, enacted 4 July 2025, added section 174A, which allows a deduction for domestic research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred during the taxable year notwithstanding section 263, with an election to capitalise and amortise them over not less than 60 months instead. Effective for amounts paid or incurred in tax years beginning after 31 December 2024.

- 26 U.S.C. §174A, Domestic research or experimental expenditures. Added by Pub. L. 119-21 §70302(a), 4 July 2025.
- https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/174A

### EVD-016 — FOMC policy rate decisions (Open Market Operations)

The FOMC raised the federal funds target range to 5.25–5.50% effective 27 July 2023, the peak of the tightening cycle, and held it there until the 25 basis point reduction of 18 September 2024 — roughly fourteen months.

- Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (US), Open Market Operations, policy tools archive.
- https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket.htm

### EVD-017 — NASDAQ Composite Index (FRED)

The NASDAQ Composite fell 36.4% from its record close of 16,057.44 on 19 November 2021 to its cycle low close of 10,213.29 on 28 December 2022.

- NASDAQ OMX Group, NASDAQ Composite Index [NASDAQCOM], retrieved from FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, 27 August 2026.
- https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/NASDAQCOM

### EVD-018 — PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor, Q4 2023

Every stage of the US private funding chain contracted at once. Deal value fell from $348.0 billion in 2021 to $170.6 billion in 2023. Exit value reached a decade low of $61.5 billion across an estimated 1,129 events. New fund commitments fell to a six-year low of $66.9 billion across 474 funds, against $169.2 billion in 2021 and $172.8 billion in 2022.

- PitchBook Data and National Venture Capital Association, Q4 2023 PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor, January 2024.
- https://nvca.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Q4-2023-PitchBook-NVCA-Venture-Monitor.pdf

### EVD-019 — US information-sector employment (BLS CES)

US payroll employment in the information sector (NAICS 51 — software publishing, data processing and telecommunications, but not computer systems design) fell from a November 2022 peak of 3,115,000 to 2,780,000 in July 2026, a decline of 335,000 or 10.8%. An official establishment survey, not a layoff tracker.

- US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Employment Statistics, series CES5000000001 (All employees, thousands, information, seasonally adjusted).
- https://data.bls.gov/timeseries/CES5000000001

### EVD-020 — Job openings, information sector (BLS JOLTS)

Job openings in the US information sector averaged 224,000 a month in 2022 and 121,000 a month in 2025, and stood at 90,000 in June 2026, against an April 2022 peak of 274,000.

- US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, series JTS510000000000000JOL (Job openings, information, total US, seasonally adjusted).
- https://data.bls.gov/timeseries/JTS510000000000000JOL

### EVD-021 — Layoffs and discharges, information sector (BLS JOLTS)

Official separations in the US information sector were 451,000 in 2022, 399,000 in 2023, 395,000 in 2024 and 447,000 in 2025 — roughly flat across the period, and without the year-to-year collapse reported by tracked-layoff counts over the same span.

- US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, series JTU510000000000000LDL (Layoffs and discharges, information, total US, not seasonally adjusted).
- https://data.bls.gov/timeseries/JTU510000000000000LDL

### EVD-022 — Hires, information sector (BLS JOLTS)

Gross hires in the US information sector fell from 1,270,000 in 2022 to 903,000 in 2025, a decline of 367,000 or 28.9%. The measure counts hiring flows, not layoff announcements.

- US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, series JTU510000000000000HIL (Hires, information, total US, not seasonally adjusted).
- https://data.bls.gov/timeseries/JTU510000000000000HIL

### EVD-023 — Tracked technology layoffs (Layoffs.fyi)

A privately maintained tracker that compiles publicly reported layoff events at technology and startup companies worldwide, revised as new reports arrive. It is not a statistical census. It records 165,269 employees in 2022, 265,660 in 2023, 152,922 in 2024, 122,606 in 2025 and 127,180 between 1 January and 24 August 2026.

- Layoffs.fyi — Tech and Startup Layoff Tracker, per-year pages, retrieved 27 August 2026.
- https://layoffs.fyi/2026-layoffs/

### EVD-024 — Announced job cuts, technology sector (Challenger, Gray & Christmas)

A count of announcements of planned job cuts by US-based employers rather than of completed separations; not an official statistic. It reports 133,988 technology-sector cuts announced in 2024, 154,445 in 2025 and 149,023 between January and July 2026 — 67% above the 89,251 announced in the same months of 2025.

- Challenger, Gray & Christmas, Job Cut Announcement Report, July 2026.
- https://www.challengergray.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Challenger-Report-July-2026.pdf

### EVD-025 — Hires rate, total private (BLS JOLTS)

The seasonally adjusted hires rate for total private employment was 3.7% in June 2026 (preliminary), a full percentage point below its June 2022 level of 4.7%: fewer positions per hundred jobs are being filled each month.

- US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, series JTS100000000000000HIR (Hires rate, total private, seasonally adjusted).
- https://data.bls.gov/timeseries/JTS100000000000000HIR

### EVD-026 — Quits rate, information sector (BLS JOLTS)

The seasonally adjusted quits rate in the US information sector was 1.1% in June 2026 (preliminary), down from 1.9% in June 2022: fewer seats are being vacated by the people already in them.

- US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, series JTS510000000000000QUR (Quits rate, information, seasonally adjusted).
- https://data.bls.gov/timeseries/JTS510000000000000QUR

### EVD-027 — Applications per opening (Greenhouse hiring benchmarks)

Applications received per open role across the reporting platform's customer base rose from 116 in 2022 to 244 in 2025, an increase of 111%. The stated dataset covers over 6,000 companies and over 640 million applications, so it measures one platform's customers rather than the labour market.

- Greenhouse, The Hire Standard: hiring benchmarks report, North America, March 2026.
- https://www.greenhouse.com/recruiting-benchmarks

### EVD-028 — Seniority mix of software postings (Indeed Hiring Lab)

Senior-level roles accounted for 69.3% of software development postings and entry-level roles for 4.5% in the first quarter of 2026, measured on one job board's postings rather than on all vacancies.

- Indeed Hiring Lab, The Labor Market Is Tilting Toward Seniority, 23 July 2026.
- https://hiringlab.indeed.com/2026/07/23/the-labor-market-is-tilting-toward-seniority/

### EVD-029 — Employment of young software developers (Stanford Digital Economy Lab)

In payroll records covering 3.5–5 million workers a month, employment of software developers aged 22–25 fell by close to 20% between its late-2022 peak and September 2025, while employment for older workers in the same occupation did not fall. This is the paper's raw descriptive series for one occupation; its headline regression result — a 16% relative decline for ages 22–25 in AI-exposed occupations, controlling for firm-level shocks — is a different figure and should not be conflated with it.

- Brynjolfsson, E., Chandar, B., & Chen, R. (2025). Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence. Stanford Digital Economy Lab, 13 November 2025.
- https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/app/uploads/2025/11/CanariesintheCoalMine_Nov25.pdf
